Industry News: Bitcoin Hovers Just Above Average Holder’s Cost Basis as Price Keeps Dipping

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.
  • The price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000.
  • It has been revealed that the margin is thin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin is trading just above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network, and a break below that level would put the average holder at a loss for the first time since early 2023, Glassnode, an onchain analytics firm posted Friday.

The price of bitcoin sat near $61,700 on Friday after sliding below $62,000. The realized price is a measure of what holders paid, not where the market trades. When bitcoin trades above it, the typical coin is sitting on a gain. Below it, the typical coin is underwater.

It has been revealed that the margin is thin. The firm stated the MVRV ratio, which compares bitcoin’s market value with its realized value, sits “just above 1.” A reading of 1 means the market price has fallen all the way to the realized price.

In a recent development, realized price values each coin at the price it last moved on the blockchain, then averages across the supply. Look Into Bitcoin describes it as bitcoin’s average cost basis. Because it tracks the price when coins last changed hands, it moves far more slowly than the market.

The MVRV ratio expresses the same idea as a multiple. Above 1, holders are in profit on average. Below 1, they are not. A reading just above 1 means the market price is only a sliver higher than what the average coin cost.

The firm did not give the exact realized price in its post, which included a chart. That leaves the exact cushion between today’s price and the average cost basis unstated. Bitcoin Magazine Pro’s full realized price chart sits behind a login, so the current level could not be confirmed independently for this report.

According to recent reports, “The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit,” the firm wrote. “The margin is thin.”.

Sources indicate that the slide has come with heavy selling from funds. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost about $541 million on Thursday, its largest one-day outflow since it released in January 2024, Bloomberg reported. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total that day.

The selling stands out against the buying earlier in the fall. Institutions piled into bitcoin ETFs through the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record, Bitcoin Magazine reported this week.

Sources indicate that leveraged traders took losses too. More than $700 million in leveraged crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, and about 86% of them were bets on higher prices. Bitcoin accounted for roughly $200 million of the total.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill remarked the drop is part of a longer downturn rather than the start of a new one. “I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another,” he said in a note dated Nov. 18.

It has been revealed that the note frames Friday’s price action as a late stage of a decline that began well before November. Butterfill pointed to whale selling that weighed on prices from late 2025, expectations of higher interest rates and weakness in technology stocks, all of which have kept buyers cautious.

“Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he remarked. “Geopolitics will have a considerable say in that.”.

Recent findings suggest that A move through the realized price would put bitcoin near the bottom edge of that range. The firm remarked holders as a group have not been in loss since early 2023.

A sustained breakout, Butterfill stated, would likely require “a change in the policy outlook, renewed whale participation or both.”.

#121620. ‘Price exposure, not the share itself’ — What do tokenized stock holders actually get?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (959 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ambcrypto ↗ Open Full Page

‘Price exposure, not the share itself’ — What do tokenized stock holders actually get?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (959 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ambcrypto

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, crypto exchanges spent the past week rolling out tokenized U.S stocks to buyers around the world.
  • One story is about tokenization, while the other is about AI stocks.
  • Industry observers note that for most people outside the U.S, buying an Apple or Nvidia stock is hard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, crypto exchanges spent the past week rolling out tokenized U.S stocks to buyers around the world. On an unrelated note, Nvidia slid by 30% from its ATH in a month following Jensen Huang’s departure. All while AMD rose — an early sign of decoupling.

One story is about tokenization, while the other is about AI stocks. However, both skirt around the same topic: a growing class of investors being handed exposure they don’t fully understand by markets that do not care to explain it.

Industry observers note that for most people outside the U.S, buying an Apple or Nvidia stock is hard. It is either expensive, tedious, or simply unavailable. Pritam Dutta, Founder and CEO of Zoth, explained the same when he spoke to AMBCrypto, stating,.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot of excitement around tokenized stocks right now. Most people outside the U.S. still can’t easily buy shares in Apple, Nvidia and the rest of the Magnificent Seven. Tokenization changes that.

Undoubtedly, for a buyer in Nigeria or the Philippines, a tokenized stock could be their first realistic route into U.S markets. But Dutta’s next point is the one that should make an investor sit up and take notice.

A lot of what’s launching gives you price exposure, not the share itself. You don’t get voting rights, and dividends depend on the platform’s terms… Too few platforms are being upfront about it.

Sources indicate that in a nutshell, investors are not buying Apple. They are buying a token that tracks Apple’s price, issued by a platform whose terms determine what else you get, subject to its discretion.

Dutta, then, reduced the entire conversation to three questions investors must ask themselves before running towards such stocks.

Who holds the real share? What happens to my dividends? What happens if the platform fails?

These are not clever questions. These are the questions you should ask before buying anything that is marketed as “tokenized.” Unfortunately, the fact that they need to be asked in the first place is a sure-shot sign of how little the platforms are disclosing.

Sources indicate that in today’s age, the access is real, but the understanding might not be. And, that gap is the hardest on buyers with the least room to make an error.

According to recent reports, nvidia fell this week while AMD rose. The easy explanation is Jensen Huang’s exit. However, Ian Weisberger, CEO of CoinRoutes, believes that there is a larger cause. He told AMBCrypto,.

The real problem is that Nvidia’s chips are becoming a commodity.

According to recent reports, for years, Nvidia and the AI boom were not seen as two separate entities, simply because of the former’s chips. That is also how the company grew to roughly 8% of the S&P 500.

This week, though the market began pulling the two apart — and within the AI sector — the separation was underway long before anyone realized.

Anyone who has built on both stacks knows the gap is closing. As the chips become interchangeable, buyers will shop on price, and the profits will move to the companies building products on top of them.

That is the concentration problem in one paragraph. When a single stock is 8% of the AI sector, millions of retail investors own a large position in it through their index funds. That is exposure they never signed up to be a part of.

The AI boom is not ending, but the era of one stock carrying the index might be.

Both stories have the same problem — the people most likely to be hurt are unfortunately the least equipped to protect themselves. Here’s why.

Sources indicate that firstly, tokenized stocks are best for an overseas buyer for whom a U.S brokerage account is out of reach. Unfortunately, that buyer is also the first to suffer losses if their platform of choice fails.

In a recent development, secondly, when it comes to artificial intelligence, the cracks are less noticeable. Most overseas retail investors own Nvidia through an index fund that was marketed to them as “diversified.” This causes the investor with the least information to hold one of the most important market bets.

As Nicolai Sondergaard, research analyst at Nansen, told AMBCrypto:.

AI and crypto draw on the same pool of risk capital, so when Nvidia sells off, the money goes to cash, not into Bitcoin.

It has been revealed that at the time of Sondergaard’s analysis, Nvidia was down about 32% from its 6th October high, Bitcoin [BTC] was 26% below its September peak, and gold was 17% off its August high. Meanwhile, the dollar was at a six-month high, and real yields were up more than 0.2 percentage points in two months.

It has been revealed that so, the investor who thought they were spread across AI and crypto was actually holding double the risk. And in the worst case, they must have not figured it out before it was too late.

According to recent reports, the same story can be crafted across different markets — the sophisticated investor can take on the risk, while the overseas investor cannot. Regardless, the product holds no difference when marketing to them.

The demand is real. The question is whether people are being sold what they think they’re buying.

The question at the end of it all is — were buyers sold a dream that was impossible to achieve? Looking further, was the promised portfolio diversification ever there at all?

Sources indicate that in the end, the retail investor’s blind spot is not ignorance. It is the industry that keeps expanding faster than investors understand what’s going on, causing them to buy the narrative and allure. Not the reality.

  • The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.
  • This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

Sources indicate that the award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

The judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

It has been revealed that kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Debuted in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

In a recent development, it’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the latest Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Sadly, Kia has no plans to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

Recent findings suggest that the 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Block Says Most Bitcoin Payments on Square Are for Coffee and Food

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (650 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block remarked in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.
  • It has been revealed that the report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S.
  • According to recent reports, food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most bitcoin payments at Square sellers are small, everyday purchases at coffee shops and restaurants, Block remarked in a new report that it hopes will inform a debate in Congress over a tax break for small crypto purchases.

It has been revealed that the report, “The State of Bitcoin Payments,” covers completed bitcoin payments at U.S. Square sellers from Nov. 1, 2025, to Oct. 15, 2026. The median payment was about $13, and the average was about $29.

According to recent reports, food and drink businesses took 72% of those payments, Block found. That is a bigger share than the category’s 67.5% slice of regular card payments on Square over the same period.

“Most bitcoin payments are small and routine,” the company wrote on X Thursday, calling the report one of the first datasets on how people spend bitcoin in the local economy.

Recent findings suggest that coffee shops and fast food businesses accounted for 62.6% of the bitcoin payments in the food and drink category, with a median payment of $9.10. Grocery stores made up a smaller share but had the highest average payment in the group, at $60.73.

Small tickets dominated. About 42% of bitcoin payments on Square were under $10, and 65.1% were under $20. Those sub-$20 payments made up just 19.1% of total payment value, though, with a few larger purchases accounting for much of the dollars spent.

According to recent reports, customers also came back. Among Cash App people who paid with bitcoin at least twice at the same merchant, the median was three purchases per customer-merchant pair. About 44% of bitcoin payments from Cash App were repeat payments, and 86% of those came within 30 days.

In a recent development, the activity was not limited to Block’s own app. External Lightning wallets such as Strike, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix and Coinbase handled 56.6% of Square bitcoin payments and about 66% of payment value, while Cash App wallets made up the rest.

Recent findings suggest that square sellers can choose how much of each sale they keep in bitcoin, and Square converts the rest to dollars automatically. Block said zero-fee processing for bitcoin payments on Square has been extended through Dec. 31, 2027. Local governments are testing similar setups, with Miami-Dade County now taking bitcoin for property taxes and converting it to dollars.

According to recent reports, block tied the data to tax policy. Under current U.S. federal rules, paying with bitcoin generally means calculating a capital gain or loss on every purchase, even a $10 coffee, the company noted.

A Morning Consult survey that Block commissioned found that 23.6% of businesses that don’t accept bitcoin cite tax and accounting complexity as a reason. That is about the same share that cite regulation, refunds or price swings. Among businesses that have considered taking bitcoin but haven’t, the figure was 27%.

Sources indicate that consumers pointed to friction, too. Morning Consult surveyed 8,669 U.S. adults who are aware of bitcoin in August. Among those who don’t own it, 29.6% said they would be more likely to pay with bitcoin if it were easier, and 15.7% of that group said they were unsure how it is taxed or regulated.

It has been revealed that block said Congress is weighing a crypto tax package and pointed to a de minimis exemption, which would exempt small gains on qualifying purchases, as one option. Industry groups have pressed lawmakers on crypto tax rules for months, with little movement so far.

The report doesn’t give totals. Block said the number of Square bitcoin payments, the number of sellers receiving them and total bitcoin payment volume are proprietary and not disclosed. Merchant lists like the 425 Los Angeles businesses that accept bitcoin offer a rough sense of reach.

“We think tax policy should account for how people spend bitcoin as well as how they hold it,” Block mentioned.

Industry observers note that the UK is carving out a role for third-party firms that make markets in spot Bitcoin. From Oct. 25, 2027, they can buy and sell on qualifying crypto trading platforms without permission to deal as principal for that activity. The Financial Conduct Authority’s final rules bar UK platform operators from making markets on their own venues.

HM Treasury made the amending regulations on Nov. 18, 2026, adding Article 9UA to the UK’s regulated activities framework. The provision excludes market making on a qualifying cryptoasset trading platform from Article 9T, which covers dealing in qualifying cryptoassets as principal. A separate part of Article 9UA excludes trading strictly for a firm’s own purposes when it provides no service to anyone else.

It has been revealed that A qualifying platform brings together multiple third-party buyers and sellers so their orders can result in trades in qualifying cryptoassets. The exclusion covers market making in those assets, including spot Bitcoin.

In a recent development, in its draft guidance, the FCA describes a market maker as a firm that stands ready to buy and sell listed assets on a continuing basis at prices it sets. The regulator proposes that responding to requests for quotes on the platform can also qualify.

CryptoSlate previously covered how the FCA’s final crypto rules govern venue access and authorization when the newly introduced regime begins.

In a recent development, operating a UK qualifying cryptoasset trading platform requires FCA authorization. The FCA’s final venue rules require operators to identify, document and monitor market-making users and disclose the terms of relevant incentives. A separate affiliate may trade on the venue under the same access rules as other users.

An operator can step between buyer and seller to execute client orders on its own platform as a matched principal when it holds the appropriate additional permission and follows venue rules that give it no discretion over how orders are matched. An operator that executes client orders against its own capital away from its own venue needs principal-dealing permission and must disclose its role and manage conflicts.

Recent findings suggest that the UK rules give distinct treatment to third-party market making, a venue trading for itself and a venue executing client orders from Oct. 25, 2027.

Market making on a qualifying platform is excluded from principal dealing. On its own venue, a UK operator needs separate permission to execute orders as matched principal.

It has been revealed that the diagram covers UK platform conduct and the principal-dealing exclusion. Other regulated activities may require separate permissions.

Compare the statutory Article 9UA exclusion with CRYPTO 6’s final rules on UK platform activities.

In a recent development, the diagram covers UK platform conduct and the principal-dealing exclusion. Other regulated activities may require separate permissions.

Firms that take orders from customers have to assess their permissions separately. Dealing as an agent or arranging deals can require permission. Firms executing or forwarding orders covered by the FCA’s rules for UK retail and elective professional clients must use a UK qualifying cryptoasset execution venue.

According to recent reports, the FCA’s application window closes Feb. 28, 2027, for eligible firms with an existing UK cryptoasset business that want transitional protection for regulated activities. Market making that falls within Article 9UA carries no principal-dealing application requirement for that activity.

The FCA’s consultation on the carve-out closed Nov. 18, 2026. Its consultation page targets January 2027 for final guidance, while the consultation paper gives spring 2027.

Bitcoin Price Crashes to $59,000 as Market Selloff Deepens

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S.
  • Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m.
  • It has been revealed that the break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower.

Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data. The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000.

It has been revealed that the break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss.

According to recent reports, wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower.

Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry.

According to recent reports, rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed. Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield.

Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

It has been revealed that some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.

JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June.BTC is now less than 4% away from a latest cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz.

Industry observers note that funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.

In a recent development, the move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session. Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.

Sources indicate that bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

Sources indicate that data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.

The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

Wagyu’s Monero-linked token plunged on Hyperliquid on Nov. 20 in a sell-off that generated about $14 million in gross proceeds for the seller, according to blockchain data firm Bitquery. The account that sent XMR1 to that wallet also created Wagyu’s Zcash-linked token, ZEC1, and held 99.97% of its supply at 13:16 UTC that day.

Industry observers note that ZEC1 trades separately from XMR1. A transfer from the shared deployer could put a large block of ZEC1 in the hands of a seller, just as the XMR1 transfers did in the Monero-linked market. The Industry Spread reported that a Nov. 21 balance check put the same account’s holdings at about 20.99 million ZEC1. The figure counts wrapped tokens on Hyperliquid. The same Hyperliquid account sent XMR1 to the seller and held almost all of the separate ZEC1 supply.

Industry observers note that the XMR1 bar compares the amount sold with the amount transferred. The ZEC1 bar shows the deployer’s share of total ZEC1 supply.

The branches show account relationships. The ZEC1 branch measures the wrapped-token balance and does not establish a transfer, native-chain reserves or redemption availability.

Recent findings suggest that bitquery’s November 20 Hyperliquid analysis counted XMR1 sales through 13:00 UTC and measured ZEC1 supply at 13:16 UTC. The XMR1 track represents 5.2 million transferred tokens, filled in proportion to 369,623 sold. The ZEC1 track represents total ZEC1 supply.

The branches show account relationships. The ZEC1 branch measures the wrapped-token balance and does not establish a transfer, native-chain reserves or redemption availability.

Sources indicate that bitquery traced three transfers totaling about 5 million XMR1 from the deployer to the selling wallet between 04:46 and 05:16 UTC. The seller had moved only a fraction of that amount through the order book by Bitquery’s 13:00 UTC cutoff. The tally covered 369,623 XMR1 sold to 420 buying accounts. The token’s spot price fell from about $500 to about $1 in roughly half an hour. The first large sales began at 04:49 UTC, and Bitquery tracked smaller sales as late as 10:28 UTC.

According to recent reports, three-quarters of the proceeds came from buy orders already on Hyperliquid’s order book. The largest buying account paid about $4 million. The buyers’ final losses depend on what they can recover.

CryptoSlate previously reported on a separate trading-key risk on Hyperliquid following the Lighter incident.

Sources indicate that wagyu’s documentation describes how users deposit native Monero or Zcash to receive XMR1 or ZEC1 on Hyperliquid. To redeem, a holder sends the wrapped token through the bridge, which pays out the corresponding native coin.

Wagyu’s homepage and its bridge page displayed a temporary outage notice on Nov. 21. The bridge widget was still checking availability, leaving it unclear whether holders could complete redemptions.

Sources indicate that wagyu operator @PerpetualCow remarked on Nov. 20 that the XMR1 deployer key had been stored on an old server at a hosting provider that was breached. He said he would personally reimburse people who lost money and relaunch Wagyu, without giving a timetable.

Bitquery found no incoming transfers from other Hyperliquid accounts to the ten largest buying accounts between 06:00 and 13:16 UTC on Nov. 20. That check ended less than half an hour after the operator’s 12:48 UTC post. Completed reimbursements remained unverified.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, in a Nov.
  • It has been revealed that claude named the writer on 68.4% of 266 standard reviews and 31.1% of 132 meta-reviews, which summarize the reviews of a submission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 correctly named the writer of 56% of 398 reviews and meta-reviews in a small test of unsigned peer reviews. Six volunteers wrote the reports. The model saw one report at a time, without web access, tools, a list of possible authors or other writing samples.

According to recent reports, in a Nov. 19 preprint, Atrey Desai and colleagues analyzed reports written between 2015 and 2026 for 26 double-blind conferences and workshops in machine learning and natural language processing. The researchers knew who wrote each report, but the reviewers’ names had never been publicly linked to them. In 19 cases, the text itself was already publicly available without a name.

It has been revealed that claude named the writer on 68.4% of 266 standard reviews and 31.1% of 132 meta-reviews, which summarize the reviews of a submission. The meta-reviews were shorter and came from just two of the six contributors. The study did not separate the effects of report length, type and authorship.

The 56% result counts each report equally, so contributors who supplied more reports had more influence on the overall figure. When the researchers gave each reviewer equal weight, Claude’s average accuracy was 49.1%. The test revealed that an unsigned report can give its writer away. Estimating how often that happens across confidential peer review would take a larger, more varied sample.

In the study, Claude Fable 5.2 saw one report at a time, without web access, tools, candidate names or extra writing samples.

Only two of the six volunteers wrote the meta-reviews.

Industry observers note that the meta-reviews were shorter. The study cannot separate the effects of report length, type and writer.

Recent findings suggest that claude Fable 5.2 received one text per attempt, without web access, tools, candidate names or additional writing samples. Both bars use a common 0% to 100% scale. The rates are reported in Table 32.

The meta-reviews were shorter. The study cannot separate the effects of report length, type and writer.

The researchers also tested 1,559 public reviews from 47 open-review journals. Claude correctly identified the reviewer in 21.4% of the 1,530 cases it answered. The paper reports 39.3% accuracy for a subset containing 789 reviews that Pangram 4.1, an AI-text detector, had labeled human or mixed. The paper’s abstract cites that filtered rate, rounded to 39%.

It has been revealed that accuracy was higher on public reviews whose writers cited their own work. Claude recorded 80.2% accuracy in the group of 106 reviews with self-citations and 17.1% in the group of 1,453 without them.

It has been revealed that claude made mistakes even in the group where it performed best. An editor or author presented with a name from Claude would still need independent evidence to establish who wrote an unsigned review. CryptoSlate has also reported on how frontier AI models handled fabricated research data. The team claims it aims to add results from a substantially larger set of anonymous peer reviews in an patch to the preprint.

  • Recent findings suggest that bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec.
  • He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pushed back Friday on calls for a bigger Federal Reserve rate hike, even as bitcoin broke below $60,000 for the first time since July and stocks sank on bets that the Fed will keep tightening into a selloff.

Recent findings suggest that bessent told CNBC he would encourage the Fed not to embrace a half-point increase at its Dec. 8-9 meeting. He cited the energy supply shock and a drop in crude prices as reasons for the central bank to hold back.

He argued that one governor now backing a 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year. Bessent mentioned it “seems somewhat peripatetic” to want the bigger increase only 11 or 12 months later. He did not name the governor.

“I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards,” Bessent said.

The comments came two days after Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC a half-point hike is probably necessary in December and that the central bank may need to “shock people.” Waller said inflation is “headed in the wrong direction, and it’s spreading out.”.

Waller is not alone. Minutes of the October meeting indicated nearly all officials expect a quarter-point hike in December, and two floated a larger one. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee also declined to rule out a bigger move on Thursday.

It has been revealed that “We’ve now had multiple months in a row of borderline disturbingly high inflation rates with little progress in the sectors where we would expect to be seeing some progress,” Goolsbee told reporters. “So everything’s always on the table.”.

It has been revealed that not everyone wants to go bigger. Latest York Fed President John Williams said Tuesday that “I don’t think the situation calls for dramatic action.” St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem has suggested as many as four hikes by the spring of 2027.

Industry observers note that the Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years and held them steady in October. Inflation has stayed hot since the Iran strikes pushed up energy prices earlier this year.

According to recent reports, citi still expects a quarter-point increase in December. Global chief economist Nathan Sheets said Thursday he does not see a need for 50 basis points despite persistent inflation. In a note Friday, the bank wrote that “Fed officials will consequently have little appetite to hike into an equity sell-off.”.

Recent findings suggest that citi expects the Fed to hold after December and begin cutting later in 2027. Traders agree on the next step: the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed a more than 98% chance of a quarter-point hike, and the 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 10 basis points to 4.95% as investors bought bonds.

In a recent development, stocks fell for another day. The Nasdaq Composite dropped more than 2% in morning trading, and the VIX volatility index topped 30, its highest level since March.

Bitcoin traded near $59,700 shortly before 11 a.m. ET, down more than 5% on the day, according to Bitcoin Magazine Pro. It broke below $60,000 for the first time since early July and is on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2022.

It has been revealed that higher rates are a headwind for assets that pay no yield, and the selloff has reached companies that hold bitcoin. Strategy’s stock fell for a sixth straight session on Thursday, and the bitcoin price has dropped roughly 25% in a month, a slide Bitcoin Magazine tracked earlier this week.

In a recent development, coinShares head of research James Butterfill tied the outlook to inflation in a note dated Nov. 18. “Our base case remains range trading around USD 60k to 90k through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives monetary policy room to ease,” he noted.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,300.

It’s available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with prices starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

Both versions measure 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm high, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly longer than the Toyota Camry.

Don’t let the price fool you, however, the vehicle is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough technology.

The newly introduced Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery that provides a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

Thanks to the second-gen Blade Batteries and BYD’s Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 70% in just five minutes. A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes.

The Seal 07 is also BYD’s first vehicle to debut with its upcoming Disus-M Intelligent Magnetorheological Body Control System.

The setup features a front double-wishbone suspension and an enhanced rear five-link suspension. It works alongside BYD’s road-surface sensors that use LiDAR, plus its iTAC 2.0 Intelligent Torque Adaptation System.

Zhang Zhuo, the general manager of BYD’s Ocean sales division, offered a better look at how the system works in real life in the video shown above.

Industry observers note that BYD said the system provides ultra-fast response times down to the millisecond. The advanced suspension system adjusts damping force across a wide range of 100 to 10,000 Nm.

Sources indicate that it’s equipped on the all-electric Flagship Seal 07 variant, while lower-priced versions have the Disus-C intelligent body control system. The top-spec EV model with the Disus-M setup starts at 172,900 yuan ($26,000). Still, not too bad for what you get.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s new interior design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added a few premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio.

Sources indicate that quite impressive for sure. What's more impressive is that GM/Cadillac first offered magnetic ride control back in 2002 (a full 24 years ago!!). It may not have been quite as advanced as this system in 2026, but still one of the most advanced suspension systems offered to date for a line of vehicles.

In a recent development, I really want this car!! I truly hope BYD will be able to sell this in the USA soon.

The Seal 07 also debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that lets drivers interact with the vehicle and manage functions remotely.

Sources indicate that higher-priced versions are available with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, which includes a roof-mounted LiDAR. The setup provides safety and convenience features like Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

For a limited time, BYD is offering a “Super trade-in price” special, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the fresh Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.

Two checks cashed on the XRP Ledger on Nov. 18 paid the same AI service in RLUSD. Payments company t54 Labs identified both as batches. In its closed October beta, t54 reported that bundling requests cut the average network fee to 0.36 drops of XRP per paid call.

Sources indicate that the checks delivered 0.31 RLUSD and 0.46 RLUSD to the same ledger address. The XRPL AI Hub, run by t54 Labs, identifies the merchant as Heurist Inference Router and classifies both transfers as batches.

Sources indicate that the first check and second check came from different payer addresses. Each had a spending ceiling of 1 RLUSD. The ledger charged 12 drops of XRP to open each check and 12 to cash it, for a total of 24 drops per pair.

A drop is one millionth of an XRP. The Hub marks payment intent as unverified in its first receipt and its second receipt. The receipts give no call counts, so the November fee per request remains unknown.

t54 Labs reported that its mainnet beta settled 213,008 paid requests across 3,162 sessions using 6,324 ledger transactions from Oct. 14 to 17. It put the average network fee at about 0.36 drops per paid request. Its benchmark was a single transaction per request at the ledger's standard minimum fee of 10 drops, which can rise under load.

According to recent reports, in t54's beta, the payer first opens a check on the ledger with a maximum amount. A session key authorizes each charge off-ledger as the agent makes paid requests. At the end of the session, the merchant cashes the check once for the amount used. Each completed session takes two ledger transactions, so adding requests to a session spreads those two fees over more charges.

According to recent reports, the beta began on mainnet in October with RLUSD as its only settlement asset. t54 claims it is limited to onboarded merchants and registered payers, and its developer guide still describes sessions as part of internal merchant testing. The public facilitator has yet to offer batch sessions, according to t54.

Industry observers note that an open check adds 0.2 XRP to the payer's reserve requirement on top of the regular 1 XRP account reserve. That amount remains in the account while the check is open. A payer with several checks open at once needs the extra reserve for each one. The reserve requirement falls when the check is cashed or canceled. Expiration alone leaves the check on the ledger until someone cancels it.

The payer opens a check, paid calls are authorized off the ledger, and the merchant cashes the check once. t54 reported 0.36 drops per paid request in its October mainnet test.

According to recent reports, the extra 0.2 XRP reserve lasts while the check is open. The two ledger fees are shared across the paid requests in a completed session.

In a recent development, the October fee average comes from t54’s closed beta. The November Heurist receipts omit request counts. Neither the reserve nor the RLUSD payment enters the fee comparison.

The lifecycle follows t54 and XRP Ledger documentation. The chart uses a common linear scale from zero. The October beta average is 0.36 drops per paid request. The 10-drop comparison assumes one standard minimum-fee transaction per request.

The ledger records show that pattern in both November examples. Each payer's count of owned ledger objects rose by one when the check opened and returned to its earlier level after cashing.

In a recent development, the RLUSD principal moves at cashing. The ceiling caps what the merchant can collect, and the payer needs enough funds when the merchant submits the check.

On Nov. 22, XRP traded at about $0.93, according to CryptoSlate’s XRP price data.

The XRPL AI Hub dashboard reports settlement value in dollars and lists registered merchants separately. t54 counts each batch as one settlement, so settlement counts can grow more slowly than paid requests.

Latest Update: Researchers Publish Security Analysis of Bitcoin’s Post-Quantum SHRINCS Proposal

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it.
  • Recent findings suggest that the analysis, dated Nov.
  • It has been revealed that SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several researchers have published a 131-page security analysis of SHRINCS, a proposed post-quantum signature scheme for Bitcoin, and are asking the wider community to look for flaws in it. Researcher Mikhail Kudinov announced the first version Thursday in a thread on X, saying the paper reduces SHRINCS’ security to the properties of its underlying hash function.

Recent findings suggest that the analysis, dated Nov. 18, estimates classical security of 121.4 to 122.7 bits for SHRINCS, though those figures rest on assumptions that include three unproven conjectures. Kudinov said the work is not finished. The team is still working on a latest analysis of a property called SM-DSPR, whose bound has so far been conjectured, and on tightening a reprogramming step and improving a bound against quantum attackers.

It has been revealed that SHRINCS is a hash-based scheme, meaning its security rests on hash functions rather than the elliptic curve math behind today’s Bitcoin signatures. It places two designs under one key: a stateful part built on FXMSS with WOTS+C, and a stateless fallback built on SLH-DSA. Because both use the same hash function, Kudinov noted, the proof has to cover both.

Signature size is the main cost. Under the draft proposal, stateful SHRINCS signatures run from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while the stateless fallback is 5,777 bytes. Schnorr signatures on Bitcoin today are 64 bytes, and ECDSA signatures typically come in around 71. Signatures take up scarce block space, so larger ones mean fewer transactions per block.

Sources indicate that the compact stateful path carries a danger. It relies on one-time keys, and if a wallet accidentally reuses one, an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal the funds. Wallet software therefore has to track the state of every key. The stateless path avoids the problem, but at a much larger size.

Jonas Nick, Blockstream’s director of research, told Isabel Foxen Duke, head of the MARA Foundation, on MARA Foundation TV that wallets must automatically fall back to the stateless path whenever a state counter could be compromised. “It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” he said. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”.

Nick also warned that heavy use of the larger signatures would weigh on the network. “We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very substantial signatures,” he stated. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”.

Industry observers note that the authors are clear that the analysis needs scrutiny. Kudinov remarked it has not been sufficiently peer reviewed, and the project’s GitHub repository warns that the documents may contain errors and should not be the sole basis for deploying SHRINCS. “We tried to be careful, but a proof of this size can have mistakes,” he wrote, asking readers to open an concern if they find one.

Sources indicate that the team also produced two results that are not specific to SHRINCS: a classical bound for a property called ITSR without reprogramming, and a quadratic quantum bound for undetectability. Kudinov said they also apply to SPHINCS+ and SLH-DSA, the hash-based schemes SHRINCS borrows from, and that they were published as separate papers.

The SHRINCS work lands as quantum risk climbs the agenda. A global securities regulators’ group this week warned that moving blockchains to quantum-resistant cryptography may be especially hard, and researchers recently built a post-quantum defense for the Lightning Network after Bitcoin’s first quantum-safe transaction was shown without a fork.

Recent findings suggest that the draft Bitcoin Improvement Proposal for SHRINCS is also open for comment. “We need all the possible feedback — engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, mentioned of it. “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise.”.

Europe’s electric car sales jump 49% as global EV sales grow

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026.
  • Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to latest data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
  • Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Global EV sales climbed 8% in October, with Europe’s battery electric vehicle (BEV) sales jumping 49% and North America posting its first year-over-year increase in 2026. But that North American rebound comes with a massive catch.

Drivers bought 2.09 million EVs worldwide last month, according to latest data from Benchmark Mineral Intelligence. That’s down 3% from September, but it brings sales for the first 10 months of 2026 to 17.5 million – up 5% from the same period last year.

Benchmark’s figures include both BEVs and plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) in the passenger-car and light-duty vehicle markets.

Recent findings suggest that europe sold 510,000 EVs in October, up 36% year over year. Fully electric cars did most of the work: BEV sales rose 49%, while plug-in hybrids grew 7%.

That puts October’s growth ahead of Europe’s 31% increase for the year so far. The region has now sold 4.5 million EVs in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that sales fell 17% from September’s record, but September got a boost from the UK’s twice-yearly registration plate change. The year-over-year figures give a clearer view of how quickly the market is growing.

Germany’s EV share topped 45% of fresh car sales, its highest level since December 2022. That earlier peak came as buyers rushed to get cars before subsidy cuts took effect. Fully electric car sales in Germany rose almost 80% from a year earlier to more than 95,000.

It has been revealed that UK EV sales increased 30%. That’s particularly notable because the Electric Car Grant was already available in October 2025, although fewer models qualified then. So this growth comes against a market that was already getting government support.

And in Portugal, EVs accounted for 55% of upcoming car sales in October, following a sharp rise in their market share over the past few months.

Sources indicate that north American EV sales rose 24% year over year to 130,000 in October, the region’s first annual increase of 2026. Sales were flat from September, while the year-to-date decline narrowed to 21%, from 24% a month earlier. The region has sold 1.3 million EVs so far this year.

US EV sales reached around 110,000 units in October.

But here’s the catch: October 2025 was the first month after the federal EV tax credit expired. The credit ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and sales dropped sharply afterward.

October 2026 is therefore being compared with a month when sales plummeted. A positive annual number doesn’t mean US demand has returned to its pre-expiration level.

“October is the first month compared against a period without the US federal tax credit, and the US market has stabilized at a lower level rather than recovered,” stated Charles Lester, Benchmark’s data manager.

The flat month-over-month figure helps tell that story: Sales have steadied, but the market is operating from a lower base.

Industry observers note that china sold 1.14 million EVs in October, up 5% from September but down 12% year over year. That annual decline was smaller than September’s 18% drop.

Sales through October reached 9.1 million, down 11%, compared with a 13% year-to-date decline at the end of September.

Recent findings suggest that even with fewer EVs being sold, their share of China’s fresh car market reached a fresh high. That’s because the wider passenger car market is shrinking faster.

Recent findings suggest that chinese automakers are continuing to produce vehicles and look overseas for buyers. Passenger car exports of newly introduced energy vehicles – China’s category covering BEVs and PHEVs – reached nearly 600,000 in October. That’s another monthly record, up from 558,000 in September.

Those exports face more pressure ahead. The EU has agreed to cap imports of Chinese-built hybrids, and China will reduce its EV export VAT rebate from 13% to 9% starting April 1, 2027.

Outside China, Europe, and North America, EV sales rose 85% year over year to 300,000 in October. Those markets have bought 2.6 million EVs so far in 2026, up 93%.

According to recent reports, australia’s sales jumped more than 200% in October, and EVs have gained market share sharply this year. But that hasn’t translated into healthy dealer profits, according to Benchmark. More brands, many of them Chinese, are competing for buyers, spreading sales across more companies and squeezing dealer margins.

Brazil’s growth has also been huge, although Benchmark cautions that some of its drivers are temporary. Importers brought vehicles in ahead of phased tariff increases, a fuel crisis pushed more buyers toward EVs, and BYD increased production at its Brazilian factory.

Recent findings suggest that nothing like consumer economics to drive sales. Local story about consumer economics: Windturbines on land is not popular. However, the locals realised they could heat their home for $300/year (in Denmark(!)) with these wind turbines and then they were tolerated! Same with cars - people gravitate to cheaper alternatives despite the more frequent charging and initial higher prices.

As the tariff increases take full effect and fuel price pressure eases, Benchmark expects those boosts to fade. BYD’s local production, which will also supply Argentina and Mexico, is set to become the main remaining support for that growth.

Senators want state-licensed firms to keep issuing stablecoins after Jan. 18

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Six senators are asking Treasury to let qualifying state-regulated stablecoin issuers keep putting newly introduced tokens into circulation while their states’ rules are under federal review.
  • Cynthia Lummis and Kirsten Gillibrand led the bipartisan November 17 letter, which Lummis’s office released November 18.
  • The proposed Section 3 rule would recognize relief for two groups with applications pending when the law takes effect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six senators are asking Treasury to let qualifying state-regulated stablecoin issuers keep putting newly introduced tokens into circulation while their states’ rules are under federal review. The GENIUS Act takes effect on January 18, 2027. Treasury’s proposal recognizes temporary relief for eligible federal applicants that get a waiver. It leaves open what happens if a state’s regulatory framework still awaits certification.

Industry observers note that sens. Cynthia Lummis and Kirsten Gillibrand led the bipartisan November 17 letter, which Lummis’s office released November 18. They asked Treasury for temporary protection during certification for issuers in states that will have a qualifying framework in place before January 18, 2028. They warned that a clearer federal route could steer issuers toward a federal license.

The proposed Section 3 rule would recognize relief for two groups with applications pending when the law takes effect. One is a subsidiary of an insured depository institution whose parent has applied on its behalf. The other is an applicant seeking to become a federally qualified payment stablecoin issuer. The primary federal regulator must grant a waiver, and its terms must cover the relevant Section 3 restriction. Relief can run for up to 12 months from the law’s effective date.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has a separate final rule that requires a written request and a substantially complete issuer application pending on or before January 18, 2027. It can grant relief on public-interest grounds or in extraordinary circumstances. Its licensing page claims it has yet to open applications or waiver requests and is awaiting clearance for its application forms.

Sources indicate that treasury’s proposal treats the first transfer that gives someone outside the issuer the right to use, transfer or redeem the token as issuance. An issuer could create tokens for its own inventory and still face a restriction when it tries to put those tokens into circulation.

The OCC waiver rule gives active issuers a route to request temporary relief before the January deadline.

It has been revealed that treasury asked whether issuers should get relief before a state files for certification or while a review is pending. Four state regulatory and legislative groups asked for such protection in October. New York’s Department of Financial Services offered a different reading. It states qualifying issuers can keep issuing if their state’s rules are substantially similar and the state files within a year, until any final denial. It wants Treasury to confirm that reading in the final rule.

In the preamble to its interim rule, the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee described the state option for issuers with $10 billion or less in consolidated outstanding stablecoin issuance as requiring a state filing and committee approval. The committee has 30 days to decide once a complete certification has been submitted. It will seek to expedite initial reviews after the Act takes effect for states that had a qualifying regime in place by January 14, 2026. New York says it expects to qualify for expedited review. The initial state filing is due within a year of the Act taking effect.

According to recent reports, the committee says it will start accepting certifications once the forms clear federal review. The paperwork record still reveals the certification forms under review. If Treasury treats committee approval as a prerequisite and offers no temporary relief, issuers that depend on the state route could have to wait to issue upcoming units.

Treasury’s proposal recognizes express federal waivers. It leaves the treatment of issuers under pending state certifications open.

A January pause could affect upcoming supply before the general platform-sales rule applies.

Foreign-issued stablecoins face separate platform requirements from January 18, 2027.

It has been revealed that the two branches map the federal waiver in proposed § 1523.4(a) and Treasury’s question about relief while state certification is pending. Newly introduced York’s legal reading comes from its October 5 comment. The dates are statutory milestones.

Foreign-issued stablecoins face separate platform requirements from January 18, 2027.

In a recent development, fresh York’s approvals show why the legal issuer matters. The state’s Greenlist and charter register identify Ripple USD (RLUSD) and WisdomTree Dollar (USDW) as approved for issuance in the state. Ripple’s November 16 terms name Ripple Custody & Trust Co., the trade name of New York-chartered Standard Custody & Trust Firm, LLC, as the RLUSD issuer.

The OCC charter record shows that Ripple National Trust Bank’s charter became effective October 26. Ripple said Standard Custody would continue issuing RLUSD, with the separate national bank authorized to manage reserves and provide custody.

Recent findings suggest that wisdomTree identifies a different Newly introduced York trust, WisdomTree Digital Trust Firm, LLC, as USDW’s issuer. For either coin, a federal waiver would have to cover issuance by the legal issuer.

In a recent development, ZUSD still appears on the Greenlist. Its issuer, GMO-Z.com Trust Company, Inc., removed the mint function in May during a voluntary wind-down. The issuer stated direct redemptions ended November 11 and that remaining balances are subject to mandatory redemption. ZUSD’s wind-down was already underway months before Treasury published its proposal.

Under the GENIUS Act, January 18, 2027 is the effective date for the U.S. issuance restriction. If a state-regulated issuer has to pause, the immediate effect would be on its ability to supply fresh units to customers and distributors. Trading already-issued tokens and redeeming them with the issuer are separate activities.

According to recent reports, starting July 18, 2028, digital asset service providers such as exchanges generally can offer or sell payment stablecoins to people in the U.S. only if the issuer is permitted or an exception applies.

In a recent development, A separate foreign-issuer provision applies from the Act’s effective date. It conditions U.S. platform availability on the foreign issuer’s ability and commitment to comply with lawful orders and reciprocal arrangements. Section 18 also provides a route for foreign issuers from comparable regimes that register with the OCC and meet other conditions.

Honda’s $2,000 electric moped is a winner. So why can’t Americans buy it?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine.
  • Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.
  • According to recent reports, we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company unveiled prepares to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda has been steadily expanding its electric motorcycle lineup, but one of its most interesting newly introduced models isn’t a flashy high-performance machine. It’s a modest little electric scooter called the Honda UC3, and with prices now dipping close to $2,000 in local markets, it’s the kind of affordable electric two-wheeler that many Americans would probably love to get their hands on.

Unfortunately, that’s probably not happening anytime soon.

According to recent reports, we first covered the Honda UC3 earlier this year when the company unveiled prepares to launch the electric scooter in Thailand and Vietnam. Designed as an electric equivalent to a 110cc gasoline-powered scooter, the UC3 is built for practical everyday transportation rather than weekend joyrides.

But don’t let its modest appearance fool you. The UC3 packs a 6 kW (8 hp) electric motor capable of reaching approximately 50 mph (80 km/h), making it more than capable of handling typical urban commuting.

Its 3.2 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery provides up to 76 miles (122 km) of range under WMTC testing. Unlike Honda’s other electric scooters that use removable batteries, the UC3 has a permanently installed battery that charges directly on the bike.

There’s also a full-color TFT display, smartphone connectivity, three riding modes, reverse gear, and a generous 26-liter under-seat storage compartment.

And perhaps most importantly, it comes from Honda, a firm with decades of experience building reliable, affordable motorcycles.

The UC3 originally debuted in Vietnam with prices starting around 78.5 million Vietnamese dong, or roughly $3,000. However, recent reports from Vietnamese dealerships show incentives bringing prices down to around 54 million dong, equivalent to approximately $2,100.

That’s a pretty compelling price for a 50 mph (80 km/h) electric scooter from one of the world’s largest motorcycle manufacturers.

But despite its appeal, Honda hasn’t confirmed any plans to bring the UC3 to the United States.

And frankly, I wouldn’t hold my breath.

Industry observers note that in much of Southeast Asia, scooters are everyday transportation, with millions of riders using them for commuting, shopping, and practically everything else. In the US, motorcycles are much more commonly recreational vehicles, and the market for small, practical scooters is comparatively tiny.

In a recent development, I'm hoping scooters like this take over the world, the sooner the better. Anyone who's travelled in any cities in Asian, India, or most of Europe, there's always a constant background whine of 2-stroke scooters, day and night.

In a recent development, I would have thought these kinds of markets would have already transitioned to EV - in addition to the annoying sound, those 2-stroke engines spew out an order of magnitude more pollution than most ICE vehicles. I guess it's been a cost issue - this scooter should be cheap enough to take over the world.

Add in the costs of US regulatory certification, establishing parts and service support, and navigating a market where many buyers expect motorcycles to handle highway speeds, and the business case becomes considerably less attractive.

That’s unfortunate, because the UC3 looks like exactly the kind of electric two-wheeler that could make a real difference in American cities.

It’s affordable, practical, fast enough for most city streets, and backed by a manufacturer that isn’t going anywhere.

Now if only Honda would give Americans a chance to buy one.

Breaking: SEC Freezes Assets in $560 Million Crypto Trading Ponzi Scheme

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bitcoinmagazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.
  • The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022.
  • Federal prosecutors in Latest York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Securities and Exchange Commission has frozen the assets of Indianapolis-based Backward Hat Capital and its two co-founders, saying the firm ran a $560 million Ponzi scheme that told investors their money would be turned into crypto and used for AI-driven currency trading.

The agency said Backward Hat, co-founders Phillip Williams and Devin Johnson, Johnson’s firm Traders Point Capital and Joseph Anderson raised the money from more than 2,000 investors starting in July 2022. A federal court granted a temporary restraining order, an asset freeze and expedited discovery to halt what the SEC called an ongoing scheme.

Federal prosecutors in Latest York and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission brought parallel cases. The SEC and CFTC suits were filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana, and the CFTC remarked the court has appointed Kevin B. Duff as temporary receiver to take control of the companies and the individual defendants’ assets.

In a recent development, according to the SEC’s complaint, Williams and Johnson sold limited partnership interests in private funds through a network of promoters, including to Williams’s former investment advisory clients. They promised a proprietary, “AI-driven” algorithm that supposedly returned at least 6% every month by trading foreign exchange.

Industry observers note that investor money, the pitch went, would first be converted into a crypto asset and then used for that arbitrage. The complaint does not name bitcoin as the asset. It says about $109 million of the roughly $210 million raised from July 2022 to September 2025 was sent to the fund’s Coinbase account and converted.

Of that, more than $56 million went to personal crypto accounts held by Williams, Johnson and a relief defendant, according to the complaint. About $40 million ended up on three platforms where some of it was used to trade other crypto assets, but little to no money was used to trade FX. After October 2025, the scheme raised about $350 million, and none of it was sent to Coinbase.

Sources indicate that the SEC stated the defendants made more than $250 million in Ponzi payments to earlier investors and moved more than $220 million to themselves. The money paid for exotic cars, expensive homes, private air travel and other businesses they owned, and helped feed Johnson’s gambling. Promoters took more than $50 million.

Sources indicate that anderson is accused of producing fake financial reports, including at least two “audit reports” and a “quality of earnings” report from a supposedly independent firm. The SEC mentioned the documents falsely claimed the returns had been verified against bank and brokerage records. It said Anderson did no audit work, was not independent and had a financial stake in the scheme.

According to recent reports, prosecutors in Manhattan charged Williams and Johnson with securities fraud, conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit securities fraud. The FBI arrested Williams in Kokomo, Indiana, and Johnson in Gilbert, Arizona, on Wednesday. Prosecutors put the total raised at more than $600 million.

“As alleged, Phillip Patrick Williams and Devin Allen Johnson promised to use investor funds for profitable foreign exchange currency trading,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald. “Williams and Johnson instead stole hundreds of millions of dollars from their investors for personal expenses and to pay off earlier investors in a Ponzi-like fashion.”.

The CFTC put the Ponzi at more than $550 million from at least 2,100 participants and said defendants kept soliciting money through at least October 2026. Its complaint seeks restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties, trading bans and a permanent injunction. The SEC is seeking injunctions, disgorgement and civil penalties.

Sources indicate that the case follows other recent enforcement actions tied to crypto-branded fraud. The SEC charged two companies in a $130 million crypto trading scheme last month, and New York sought a $1.37 billion judgment against the operators of the NovaTech Ponzi scheme. In August, the CFTC charged Goliath Ventures with a $400 million bitcoin fraud.

Anne McKinley, acting associate director of the SEC’s Chicago Regional Office, mentioned the promise of “a low-risk, high rate of return on a purportedly complex investment should make all potential investors stop and think before investing their money.”.

Bithumb suspended deposits and withdrawals of the CYBER token after flagging signs of a possible security matter. The exchange said customers could still trade CYBER already held in their accounts. Kraken separately warned of possible delays for CYBER deposits sent over the Optimism network.

Bithumb set the cutoff for 2:18 a.m. Korea time on Nov. 22, or 17:18 UTC on Nov. 21. Seven minutes after the scheduled cutoff, the exchange confirmed that the pause was in effect. The lanes show service status based on the dated exchange notices. Line lengths do not represent the duration of a pause or delay.

Industry observers note that for users who had already sent CYBER to Bithumb, the cutoff mattered because sending a deposit and seeing it credited to an account can happen at different times. Bithumb remarked network congestion or slow confirmations could hold up credit even for transfers sent before the cutoff. It said it would credit deposits received during the suspension in sequence once service resumed.

Industry observers note that customers who had requested a withdrawal before the cutoff and were still waiting for it to complete faced a separate process. Bithumb noted it would run system checks and process those requests in sequence, which could delay the account revision. The exchange’s processing note applied to requests already in its system when the suspension took effect. Newly introduced CYBER withdrawals remained subject to the pause.

In a recent development, bithumb said it would reopen transfers once the network was stable and would post the reopening in the same notice. It gave no reopening time.

Recent findings suggest that kraken flagged possible CYBER deposit delays on Optimism at 19:59 UTC on Nov. 21 and said its other funding methods were operating normally.

#121575. Latest Update: Morning Minute: Anthropic IPO Pops, Sinks Markets

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (613 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Decrypt ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Morning Minute: Anthropic IPO Pops, Sinks Markets

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (613 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner.
  • It has been revealed that the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.
  • A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

It has been revealed that the largest base IPO deal ever priced at $83 a share Wednesday night, opened Thursday morning at $111.50, and briefly pushed Anthropic’s fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion. The stock finished at $97.17, up 17% from the offer and down 13% from where it opened (it has since fallen about 15% to $88).

A 17% first-day gain on an $81.34 billion raise is a successful listing by any normal standard.

The rest of the market did not fare as well.

The Nasdaq fell 2.06%. The S&P 500 dropped 1.9%. The Dow lost 2.17% and closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. Tech had rallied before the bell on the listing and reversed by the afternoon.

MD fell 7.73%. Nebius dropped 7.8%. CoreWeave lost 5%. Nvidia slid 3.4% despite beating earnings last week. Oracle, Micron, Broadcom and Microsoft all finished lower. The biggest AI listing in history happened, and AI infrastructure was the worst place to be holding.

Joe Maher at Capital Economics put it plainly: “Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks.”.

Crypto went with it. Bitcoin fell to $61,500, its lowest since early July. That’s a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be the longest run since the nine-week stretch in 2022. Eth hit the $1,750 level, down 28% in thirty days. Gold fell to a fourteen-month low. Silver dropped 3%.

When Bitcoin, equities and gold all sell off on the same session, the common factor is usually the discount rate.

That’s the Fed. Chris Waller spent this week making the case for fifty basis points in December, and the minutes indicated he isn’t alone. FxPro’s Alex Kuptsikevich described the market as spooked by “the spectre of a double rate hike” and pointed out Bitcoin is now more than 7% below its 200-week moving average, the deepest it has traded below that line in three years.

So where does this leave us heading into next week?

Start with what an $81 billion IPO actually does to a market. That money came from somewhere. Add the separate $26 billion private placement from Nvidia, Google, AMD and four other suppliers, and roughly $107 billion of capital got committed to a single name in one day. Kuptsikevich raised the possibility that the listing absorbed the riskiest money in the system, and that if so, some of it rotates back out once the allocation settles.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the bull case for crypto over the next few weeks. It requires the Fed to cooperate.

For the bear case, one can simply look at SpaceX.

It has been revealed that spaceX priced at $135 in June, opened at $150, and closed its first day up 19%. Then it kept running, hitting $225.64 four days later, up 67% from the offer. The unwind started the following session. By June 22 it had fallen 16% in a single day and sat 31% off the high. By mid-July it traded below its IPO price. By late July it was down roughly 50% from the peak.

That would project out to a market low around Christmas time, which is actually how the 2018 midterm cycle played out. Will history repeat itself? We will find out soon enough. In the interim, expect volatility.
